content: The treatment guidelines for tuberculosis (TB) in children with multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB) have shown an overall treatment success rate of 78%, with 75% success in confirmed cases and 89% in clinically diagnosed cases. Proper treatment of children with MDR or rifampicin-resistant TB (MDR/RR-TB) using World Health Organization (WHO)-recommended regimens is critical for achieving successful outcomes and preventing further drug resistance. For children under six years of age with MDR/RR-TB, an all-oral treatment regimen containing bedaquiline may be used, though this is a conditional recommendation based on very low certainty of evidence. This complements existing WHO recommendations for shorter and longer regimens containing bedaquiline. Shorter all-oral regimens (9–12 months) with bedaquiline are recommended for eligible patients with confirmed MDR/RR-TB who have not been exposed to second-line TB medicines for more than one month and do not have fluoroquinolone resistance. For patients aged 18 years or older, bedaquiline is strongly recommended as part of longer MDR-TB regimens, while for those aged 6–17 years, its inclusion is conditionally recommended. Historically, bedaquiline was the first new TB drug in over 40 years, receiving accelerated approval by the U.S. FDA in 2012 for adults with MDR-TB when no other effective treatment options were available. WHO issued interim guidance in 2013, recommending bedaquiline for adults under specific conditions. By 2019, after reviewing new evidence, WHO recommended bedaquiline for inclusion in longer MDR-TB regimens for adults and adolescents aged 6–17 years. The shorter all-oral bedaquiline-containing regimen replaced earlier regimens that included injectable agents. Evidence from pediatric studies, including TMC207-C211 and IMPAACT P1108, has supported the use of bedaquiline in children under six years of age. Although data are limited, findings suggest that cardiac safety signals in young children are similar to those in adults. A pediatric individual patient data (IPD) analysis also showed that bedaquiline use was associated with shorter treatment durations and reduced use of injectable TB drugs. The development of child-friendly formulations of bedaquiline, such as 20 mg scored tablets, has facilitated its use in younger children. These tablets can be taken whole, dispersed in water, or mixed with food to improve palatability. Studies have shown that the bioavailability of bedaquiline is maintained when tablets are crushed and suspended in water. Co-administration with high-fat meals optimizes drug absorption. WHO guidelines recommend that children with MDR/RR-TB who meet eligibility criteria should receive the shorter all-oral bedaquiline-containing regimen. This regimen includes bedaquiline for six months, combined with other TB drugs such as levofloxacin/moxifloxacin, ethionamide, ethambutol, high-dose isoniazid, pyrazinamide, and clofazimine for four months, followed by five months of treatment with levofloxacin/moxifloxacin, clofazimine, ethambutol, and pyrazinamide. Eligibility criteria exclude children with extensive TB disease, severe extrapulmonary TB, or resistance to key drugs in the regimen. For children not eligible for the shorter regimen, individualized longer regimens should be constructed based on drug susceptibility patterns and disease severity. Monitoring for treatment response and safety is essential, including regular clinical follow-up, weight and height monitoring, and drug dosage adjustments as needed. Efforts should also focus on improving case detection and ensuring access to child-friendly regimens. The use of bedaquiline in children requires careful consideration of potential adverse effects, such as QT interval prolongation, and appropriate safety monitoring, including electrocardiography (ECG) and electrolyte testing. Despite these challenges, the introduction of all-oral regimens is expected to improve treatment outcomes, reduce adverse events, and facilitate decentralized care delivery.
